articles.title: In Mayday, Ryan Reynolds Treads Familiar Sarcastic Territory, But Kenneth Branagh's Kooky Ex-KGB Agent Elevates the '80s-Style Buddy Comedy
articles.summary: Mayday Review: Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh team up in this likeable Cold War buddy action-comedy.
articles.body:
Mayday will be released on Apple TV on Friday , September 4.

The 1980s were rife with buddy comedies, and Mayday fits neatly within that genre, with Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh playing a US Navy pilot and an ex-KGB agent, respectively, who traverse planes, trains, and automobiles to escape Soviet Russia.

While many Hollywood movies of that era were rife with anti-Russian sentiment, from Red Dawn to Rambo III, writing-directing duo Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley take a more Spies Like Us approach to the Cold War, serving up a sometimes amusing yet boisterously action-packed reflection on geopolitical tension.

Set in 1987, a year after the release of the cinematic jingoism that was Top Gun, the film features Reynolds as Lieutenant Troy Kelly, eagerly filling the shoes of Tom Cruise's Maverick, albeit with his brand of deadpan humor – a humor here that rarely colors outside the lines of what we've seen him do before. Troy goes rogue to save his wingman's faulty plane, claims to be the best pilot of his unit and loves that Top Gun's popularity means he can queue-jump his way into any club. He applies that ego and arrogance to his dim perception of Russia and its people. "You can't reform something that is fundamentally broken," he says frankly. "It's not a society, it's a prison… silence is complicity."

Soon he's enlisted for a covert mission to co-pilot a spy plane, the Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird, to capture images of missile silos 1200 miles inside the Soviet border. Thanks to the in media res opening, we already know the operation goes sideways. After a brief but effectively thrilling sky battle with Russian fighter pilots, the so-called "beast" of his plane becomes fiery debris on the floor of a snow-laden forest, with an injured Troy clocking a mysterious man approaching before he blacks out.

Troy wakes up in the cabin of Nikolai Ustinov, or "Nick" as he prefers, and the first thing he sees is Cruise's face on a Top Gun poster pinned to the wall. American militarist propaganda has penetrated the Iron Curtain, and given the film's lack of definitive identification of the rogue nation, it's easy to understand why it's Nick's favorite film. This is Branagh's third Russian action role in recent memory, after playing Viktor Cherevin in Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit and Andrei Sator in Tenet , so it's refreshing to see him put those years of vocal coaching to more heroic use.

His Russian Americophile is less an overtly eccentric counterpart to Reynolds' straight(er) man but one with an earnest, subtly quirky appreciation of American "democracy, culture and food." There's also a lack of bravado when he outmanoeuvres both Troy and, later, patrons of a bar, in some neatly executed fight sequences. Both scenes employ wide shots and minimal edits to rivetingly capture how formidable Nick's combat skills are, adding another layer to the Branagh character, whose kind face should not lead one to mistake him for a man to be trifled with.

The rest of the film functions as a road movie, tracking their journey across Russia to find a means of escape, now that they are both enemies of the state, while being hunted by KGB official Alexander Volkov (Marcin Dorociński). He's far less menacing than, say, Christoph Waltz's Hans Landa from Inglourious Basterds, but still functions as an intimidating antagonist. Yet as much as it offers up action set-pieces like a face-off with a train full of Russian soldiers and a car chase involving a nuclear transporter in central Moscow, what's most compelling is how the very idea of American exceptionalism is dismantled. By breaking bread with common folk who welcome them into his home, conversing with Nick's activist daughter Anna (Maria Bakalova) and learning of a government cover-up that affected him personally, both Troy's prejudices and worldview crumble.

That Bruce Springsteen's Born in the USA album is as much of a running reference as Top Gun enriches the film's thematic core. Maybe it would have been too on-the-nose to include the record's eponymous anti-war song, but the fact that it's Nick's favourite cassette tape and one that Troy would prefer not to listen to for a 12-hour ride highlights the complexities and potential dysfunction of the American identity – as well as the universality of the Boss's love and lament for the working class. Borders and oceans might separate warring states, but the proletariat are very much the same: everyday people, suffering under government propaganda and class oppression.

Mayday doesn't get too deep in the weeds of political bureaucracy beyond what is required to push the plot forward, and perhaps its conclusion is a little too rosy. But that's Hollywood for you; idealism trumping reality so you can leave with a little more hope and understanding than despair.

articles.title: ‘It’s Not a Revolutionary Thing for an RPG to Have’ — Fable Explains the Very Obvious Reason as to Why Its Hero Design Has Changed
articles.summary: Fable's game director Ralph Fulton spoke to us at gamescom 2026 about character customization and confirms: Yes, it's in there.
articles.body:
Character creators are no new thing when it comes to video games, especially RPGs. Fable is just one in a very long line of adventures allowing you to sculpt a hero in your image, but when it comes time to showcase a game ahead of time, decisions need to be made.

From its initial reveal onward, we’ve become accustomed to seeing multiple chosen hero appearances throughout trailers and gameplay videos, of all shapes, sizes, and genders. But that first female hero is who has become the poster child for Playground’s reboot, with some people deciding it would be a perfectly normal thing to do to complain about her not being conventionally “attractive” enough.

Well, at gamescom 2026, the Forza Horizon studio revealed a new extended look at quest gameplay taking place in Albion’s capital of Bowerstone, in which the player hero took the form of a woman we hadn’t seen before. A response to online backlash or just a simple example of the variations available when playing around with Fable’s character creator? I asked game director Ralph Fulton.

“Earlier this year, we obviously revealed that we have had some customization in our game,” Fulton explains. “It's not a revolutionary thing for an RPG to have, but nevertheless, there was some speculation that we didn't, and we were happy to reveal: Yes, we did.”

Since then, in the assets we've put out; our showcase trailer, the live gameplay video we put out in June and both of our assets here, we've been happy to start just cycling through some of the characters you can select and customize using that tool. The girl that you see in the theater demo that we're showing today is just another one of the characters that you can select and customize in the game. And you know what? People like her, I'm delighted.”

Fable will launch on February 23, 2027, and you’ll have the freedom to make your character look however you like. It really is that simple.

For more on the RPG, you can check out not one, but two previews from gamescom 2026, where I gave my impressions of the new quest gameplay , plus my thoughts on its combat having played it .

articles.title: 'We're Improvisation-Based': Avengers: Doomsday Directors Defend Shooting Film Without a Finished Script
articles.summary: Avengers: Doomsday directors Joe and Anthony Russo have defended their decision to film the upcoming Marvel blockbuster without a finished script, with further tweaks to the movie taking place on set during shooting.
articles.body:
Avengers: Doomsday directors Joe and Anthony Russo have defended their decision to film the upcoming Marvel blockbuster without a finished script, with further tweaks to the movie taking place on set during shooting.

While this isn't the first MCU movie to evolve during production, Doomsday is undoubtedly one of Marvel's most challenging projects to date, with a vast cast of characters to balance, sky-high expectation to meet, and a sense that the return of Chris Evans and Robert Downey Jr. is something of a 'break glass in case of emergency' moment after a series of middling previous movies.

Word that pieces of Doomsday's intricate puzzle are being made up on the fly has naturally sparked concern among some fans, something that the Russos themselves have now sought to address.

The Most Surprising Avengers and Marvel Characters Not Announced for Doomsday

"We always view the script as a living organism," says Joe Russo said, as reported by the Associated Press . "We're improvisation-based, rehearsal-based directors. We like to see what the actors bring to the characters, and sometimes you don't get the actors until a few days or few weeks before you shoot them. And a lot of the time, that's when the magic happens."

With so many characters in the mix, there's some sense to seeing which groups or pairings of actors end up having the most chemistry on set, and there's no suggestion that the main plot beats of the movie aren't locked down ahead of time. Here, the Russos seem to be talking more about specific lines of dialogue or character moments that may arise organically on set.

Avengers: Doomsday Trailer: First Look at Doctor Doom

Still, with just over three months to go until Avengers: Doomsday releases, the Russos are still tinkering with the movie. It's understood that further reshoots are now taking place with additional and returning cast members ( Hawkeye actor Jeremy Renner has teased his involvement ), tacked on to the production window that will soon begin for next year's Avengers: Secret Wars.

How will it all turn out? We don't have long until Doomsday itself on December 18 when the movie finally arrives in theaters.

Officially Licensed WD SN850P 1TB PS5 SSD for $179.99

WD SN850P 1TB PCIe Gen4 x4 M.2 SSD with Heatsink (up to 7,300MBps)

The WD SN850P was made specifically for the PS5 console. That means it fulfills all of Sony's requirements, like a minimum read speed of 5,500MB/s, a PCI-Express Gen4x4 interface, and a slim yet effective heatsink that fits within the confines of the PS5 bay. It's officially licensed by Sony which means WD paid to have the PS5 logo gloriously emblazoned on its stick. No, you'll never see it once it's installed and no, it won't make your PS5 any more special, but it's there.

Of course the SN850P is also a great option as a boot drive for your gaming PC. It's one of the faster PCI-E Gen4 SSDs on the market with transfer speeds of up to 7,300MB/s read and 6,600MB/s write. The SN850P also has a dedicated LDDR4 DRAM cache. Pretty much every other SSD at this price point is DRAM-less and relies on HMB, or system memory, as a less expensive alternative. It doesn't make much of a difference in a PS5 console but PC users might notice it.

The built-in heatsink means you don't have to go out and buy one and install it yourself, even though it's not that hard and not too expensive to do so. There are a few other SSD drives at a similar price, but most of them are from brands that you've probably never heard of.

Some of the best DC superhero movies going back five decades are collected in a new 4K steelbook library case bundle. It’s called the limited-edition DC Villains 6-Film collection, and it features movies starring Superman, Batman, Aquaman, and more. Perhaps more fittingly, the movies also star villains like Joker, Catwoman, the Riddler, and Lex Luthor.

The collection is up for preorder for $139.99 exclusively at Amazon , with a release date of October 27.

DC Villains 6-Film Limited Edition Steelbook Library Case (4K UHD)

The movies range from the 1979 Christopher Reeves classic Superman: The Movie to Matt Reeves' 2022 masterpiece The Batman . Those movies are great, as are the four in between, including the two Tim Burton Batman films. See the full list of movies included below.

While the movies are obviously the main focus here, including the iconic villains the heroes fight, the packaging is also a key component of the collection. articles.title: Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 Review So Far
articles.summary: Another glorious day in the corps.
articles.body:
Perhaps no movie was primed to be a video game more than Aliens. A bunch of marines with guns up against hordes of monstrous beasties? That’s a video game, baby. That was true for the first Aliens: Fireteam Elite, a game I enjoyed but didn’t stick with for too long, and it’s also true of its sequel, which freshens that returning structure up with things like an additional player and a new class. I’m not done with Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 yet (the joys of international travel to Gamescom, I reckon), but I’ve played enough to start laying down thoughts like one of my squadmates is spiriting for an objective and my words are covering fire. The short version is this: I’m having a good time with my friends, but I am curious how long we’ll want to play after the credits roll.

You don’t have to be familiar with the original to understand what’s up here: the USS Endeavor received a transmission from a very sick-looking woman named Dr. Pearce based on LV-558, a Weyland-Yutani mining colony overrun by Xenomorphs. The marines sent in Fireteam Banshee, an elite squad, to contain the situation. They’ve all gone missing. Your Marine has been transferred to the Endeavor to bring them home and figure out what the hell is going on.

The first game wasn’t huge on story, and it doesn’t bog down Fireteam Elite 2 either. Between missions, you’ll hang out on the Endeavor and chat with your squad. There’s Shipp, the Endeavor’s CO; Ko, your tough-as-nails, no-nonsense squad leader; Piper, an analyst who is new to boots-on-the-ground work and a little nervous as a result; Esther, the ship’s android; Raptor, your dropship pilot with terrible (and I do mean terrible ) jokes; and Wrench, your mechanic/weapons specialist/shopkeeper who dispenses rad bird facts.

I enjoy the crew, even if you only really interact with them from the waist up in very “look at their face while they talk to you” scenes. My only qualm is that, because they’re mostly just the voice in your ear on missions, there’s not much room for camaraderie – and when there is, everyone’s… too nice? One of the best parts of Aliens is that the characters don’t always get along, and while I think it’s great that Ko roasts Raptor (and you), I wish these characters razzed each other a bit more. It adds flavor, you know?

Like its predecessor, Aliens Fireteam Elite 2 is a class-based, co-op-focused shooter. (You can play it solo, but you’ll be teamed up with The Alphabet Boys: CPU-controlled androids named Alpha, Beta, and Gamma.) You’ve got six classes to choose from, many of which have their own Aliens analogue. Duelist is Hicks; Marauder is Vasquez; Medic is Dietrich (there’s a deep cut for you); and so on. My favorite was the all-new Specialist, which allows you to combine the features of multiple classes. Say, for instance, you want the special abilities of the Machinist (their turret and floating bodyguard drone) but also like the Marauder’s smartgun, which is one of my early favorites. Well, the Specialist will let you do that. It’s rad. That’s not to say there’s no benefit to sticking with the traditional classes; they have modifiers and special abilities that you’ll only get by leveling that class. But if you want to do some tweaking, Specialist is your guy (or gal).

The missions themselves are pretty standard fare for the genre, but they are fun. Drop into a Weyland-Yutani nightmare, hunt for intel/break stuff/complete other objectives, kill some monstrosities, hold out until you can get out, and then get out. It’s a fun loop, especially with friends, and is set apart from other games like it by how many different kinds of Xenomorphs there are.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 – Meet (Some of) the Enemies

Runners go down quickly, so they’re probably not worth spending anything fancy or consumable on (like grenades or mines or special ammo) – but they come in big groups and they’re fast little buggers, so you can get overwhelmed quickly. Spitters like to sit back and shoot acid from afar. Then you have the big dudes: the Warriors who will pick you up and try to get you with their second mouth; the hit-and-run Drones (think the Alien from the original Alien) who leap from the shadows and retreat from fire; large red Xenos called Prowlers that pounce on you, and so on. Figuring out the right answer for everything while managing your limited resources is a lot of fun, and Fireteam Elite 2 isn’t scared to throw everything at you in the big moments.

If that wasn’t enough, certain missions also ask you to deal with Wey-Yu synthetics. These require a more methodical “take cover, approach carefully” strategy, where the Xenos will just have you running for your lives. It’s a nice change of pace.

My favorite thing, aside from the happy brain chemicals released from acquiring the M41A1 Pulse Rifle used in the film (you start with a newer model) and the sound it makes, are decals. See, you can customize your armor, which is already cool, but you can also add decals that you can move, rotate, and resize. I like the dropship I’ve attached to my Pulse Rifle and the heartbeat monitor that I’ve slapped on my breastplate, but I’m still searching for Vasquez’s Adios because I want to slap it on my smartgun. Feels right, you know? So far, I’m quite enjoying my time with Fireteam Elite 2, even if it doesn’t reinvent the wheel. It’s best with three friends (the squad size is now four marines, up from the original’s three, so your usual squad can all play instead of one person being perpetually sad), but it’s solid enough solo. Let me get to the bottom of this round of Weyland-Yutani’s startlingly bad decisions, and I’ll have a score for you. So far, however, I can confirm that it is in fact a bug hunt.

articles.title: Final Fantasy Maker Square Enix Denies Rumors That It's Going Private
articles.summary: Square Enix has spoken out to address rumors that it's going private.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy developer Square Enix has spoken out to address rumors that it's going private.

Japanese business magazine Sentaku recently reported that Square Enix was looking into going private, leading to a nearly 12% increase in the company's stock price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. But this is not the case, Square Enix has said, responding to the claim.

"The September issue of the monthly magazine Sentaku carried a report regarding the possibility of Square Enix Holdings Co., LTD. (the 'Company') going private. However, this information was not announced by the Company," Square Enix said in a statement . "No consideration is currently being given within the Company to taking the Company private."

The news comes amid wider consolidation across the gaming industry. EA was recently acquired by a Saudi Arabian investment group and taken private, which has led to concerns from both fans and EA employees about what its new owners will do. Will they continue to invest in single-player games from BioWare and leverage beloved IP like Dead Space, or will they go heavy on microtransactions and live-service games? It'll be a while before we can really see the effects of the acquisition and EA's decision to go private, but naturally, a report like this for Square Enix can lead to rampant speculation about the company's future.

Square Enix itself has made a lot of changes this decade, with arguably the biggest adjustment being when it off-loaded a lot of its western studios, such as Crystal Dynamics and Eidos Montreal, in 2022 . These teams were acquired by Embracer Group, meaning Square Enix no longer has the rights to franchises like Tomb Raider and Deus Ex. The company has also undergone multiple rounds of layoffs over the last few years, but has managed to soldier on.

articles.title: Disney Was Working On Its Own Smash Bros.-Like Fighting Game, Confirms Ex-Concept Artist
articles.summary: Former Disney Interactive concept artist Ken Christiansen confirmed that Kingdom Hearts inspired a Smash Bros.-like crossover fighting game that never got off the ground.
articles.body:
Former Disney Interactive concept artist Ken Christiansen confirmed that Kingdom Hearts inspired a Smash Bros.-like crossover fighting game that never got off the ground.

In 2013, Christiansen posted a slew of artworks to his online portfolio , some of which showed rough sketches of various Disney characters facing off in battle. It sparked the idea that Disney had possibly toyed with a crossover fighting game — something that Christiansen has now confirmed.

Speaking with Time Extension in a September 1 interview, Christiansen opened up about the surprising way Kingdom Hearts helped bring the idea to life, though it ultimately never came to fruition. In fact, it was difficult for Kingdom Hearts to get approved in the first place, as Disney execs were hesitant to combine some of the brand’s most iconic properties.

"One of the reasons Kingdom Hearts was so difficult to get started was because Disney was so reluctant to have that possibility of crossing over The Lion King into The Little Mermaid world," he explained. "That was the main hangup for Disney America. They couldn't get over that. So, I think there was maybe just a little bit of butting of heads, but it all worked out in the end. All of the creatives, though — like me, the other artists, and the producers — we all thought it was the greatest idea in the world. Like, 'Yeah, let's cross over everything.'"

"Since Kingdom Hearts already kind of broke that mold, producers would say, 'Hey, what if we say they're action figures, and we kind of take the same conceit as Toy Story, but have them fight each other instead?' Then, we can have all these action figures of Disney characters from Tarzan, The Lion King, and Treasure Planet, and it can be this Smash Brothers kind of thing. The title of that concept was 'Disney's Action Figure Face Off."

Unfortunately, this game never came to be; Time Extension reports that the project only reached the prototype stage before Disney ditched the idea in favor of movie and TV tie-in games.

With this in mind, the concept art shared to Christiansen’s portfolio makes us even more wistful for this game that never happened. The artwork showed 1v1 battles between eight different characters: Captain Hook vs Beast, the Sheriff of Nottingham vs King Louie, Ursula vs John Silver, and the Queen of Hearts vs the Horned King. Some of these characters are seriously deep cuts (we’d never expect to see the Horned King in any major Disney offering these days, let alone the Sheriff of Nottingham), and it makes us wonder who’d get chosen if such a game were to actually get made in the modern day.

Ken Christiansen's Concept Art for Disney's Smash Bros.-Like Fighting Game

"Often, when we were pitching a game at Disney, what they wanted from us was these gigantic presentation boards with art all over it. So you would get these big, six- or eight-foot-long boards that were maybe four feet high, like one-inch-thick foam core, and then over it were all these pieces of artwork printed out with big logos. So it was a big visual impact kind of thing. This was all so that you could walk the executives through the game. This led to things that did come out, like Disney's Extreme Skate Adventure,” he continued.

"Over my four years at Disney, I worked on so many concepts that never happened," said Christiansen. "I think that if there was a movie or a TV show, I probably carried it through, like Treasure Planet, Atlantis, Peter Pan 2, or Kim Possible — those games got money — or Pixar stuff like Buzz Lightyear and Monsters, Inc. But there was so much discussion about, 'What do we do with all these properties that we have?' So there's a lot of concept stuff for things that made it out.”

Speaking of Disney and games, an extended gameplay trailer for Kingdom Hearts IV was shown at D23 this year, showing off the Land of the Dead from Coco and a closer look at the modern city of Quadratum. KHIV is expected to launch in late 2027, a release window that director Tetsuya Nomura says Square Enix is firmly set on.

articles.title: Eren Yeager's English Voice Actor Literally Dislocated His Jaw to Pull Off One of Attack on Titan's Most Iconic Moments
articles.summary: Bryce Papenbrook, the English voice actor for Eren Yeager, claimed that he literally dislocated his jaw in order to realistically sell one of the most intense moments in Attack on Titan.
articles.body:
Bryce Papenbrook, the English voice actor for Eren Yeager, claimed that he literally dislocated his jaw in order to realistically sell one of the most intense moments in Attack on Titan.

Warning: Spoilers for Attack on Titan follow!

Season 2 of Attack on Titan contains one of the most iconic scenes in the entire show. In this scene, Eren speaks with fellow Scouting Legion recruits Reiner and Bertholdt after a long, arduous series of events. This particular moment reveals a major betrayal from the two soldiers, who admit that they are the Titan-shifters who broke through the wall all those years ago, resulting in untold deaths and the tragic demise of Eren’s mother.

If you’re a sub-only viewer, you’ve been familiarized with Yuki Kaji’s masterful take on the line, “You damn traitors!” but Bryce Papenbrook is also a heavy-hitter here. In fact, he was so dedicated to portraying Eren’s sadness at Reiner and Bertholdt’s betrayal that he literally inflicted physical pain upon himself by dislocating his jaw.

Attack on Titan Final Season The Final Chapters Special 1 Images

Papenbrook revealed this startling information during a panel at Anime NYC this August, drawing confusion from fellow panelist and voice actor Cristina Vee.

“In that moment, he’s more unhinged than ever before. So I literally unhinged my jaw before that take, because I wanted that pain to come through,” he explained.

“What do you mean — physically unhinged? On purpose?” Vee asked, clearly stunned.

“Yeah,” Papenbrook answered. “Like, physically pushing my jaw out of place to force pain into the feeling because of how Eren was feeling in that moment. For Eren, I really wanted to feel what he was feeling, so in Season 1, when he bites his hand, I bit my hand so hard I left bruises.”

Bryce Papenbrook, 'ATTACK ON TITAN' English voice actor for Eren Yeager, reveals he dislocated his jaw to record Eren's voice lines during the big Season 2 reveal "I literally unhinged my jaw before that take, because I wanted that pain to come through" pic.twitter.com/dVCcx3BiHw — Anime Updates (@animeupdates) September 2, 2026

Bryce Papenbrook, 'ATTACK ON TITAN' English voice actor for Eren Yeager, reveals he dislocated his jaw to record Eren's voice lines during the big Season 2 reveal "I literally unhinged my jaw before that take, because I wanted that pain to come through" pic.twitter.com/dVCcx3BiHw

Fans were left equal parts shocked and impressed by Papenbrook’s dedication to the job, with one writing on X, “Dub hate is so insanely forced, ‘cause how do people see this and call it bad?”

“He really didn’t have to, but I still love when actors get into the role,” another said.

“And before you ask, yes, it was that serious,” yet another joked. (I have to agree — while I greatly prefer the original Japanese version of the anime, this particular scene necessitated extremely intense emotion from Papenbrook’s part, and he absolutely nailed it here.)

While Attack on Titan has finally completed its journey, there’s still more to come from the beloved anime series, as Attack on Titan 3 the game is set to launch on December 3, 2026, letting players make their own character and fight through the events of the show’s final season.

articles.title: Andrew Garfield Historical Drama The Uprising Gets a Fortnite Crossover
articles.summary: Fortnite is officially crossing over with Andrew Garfield’s medieval rebellion film The Uprising, including historical melee weapons and film-inspired cinematic endings unique to each outcome.
articles.body:
Nothing screams Fortnite like the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 , am I right?

Focus Features announced Wednesday that the new movie The Uprising , starring Andrew Garfield, is now available to play as a custom experience on Fortnite ahead of the Paul Greengrass-directed film’s theatrical release on September 10.

Even for Fortnite – which has a long history of pop cultural collaborations including Star Wars , Marvel , DC , LEGO , The Witcher , Godzilla and Kong , Stranger Things , John Wick , and Back to the Future – The Uprising is a curious film to cross over with.

The period drama – which may or may not (still) be a Robin Hood origin movie – chronicles the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, which was led by historical figures Wat Tyler (played by Shogun’s Cosmo Jarvis) and John Ball (played by Jamie Bell). Andrew Garfield’s lead character, Ploughman, is meant to represent the Everyman peasant pushed by misfortune into taking up arms against the crown.

According to the official announcement, “the free Unreal Editor for Fortnite (UEFN) experience, developed by Sawhorse Productions and published by Genesis Studios, immerses players in the heart of the legendary uprising, bringing the film's world to life through a large-scale multiplayer battle inspired by the events and visual landscape of The Uprising.”

“Set in 1380s England, the custom 5v5 payload-escort experience pits Rebels against Kingsmen in a battle for London’s gates. Rebel forces must push a battering-ram through four escalating map phases, advancing from muddy farmland to the fortified city walls, while Kingsmen fight to stop their advance before time expires. Players wield era-inspired melee weapons and bows, earn in-match currency and strategically upgrade their health, speed, and damage throughout the fight.”

Focus says The Uprising experience “culminates in film-inspired cinematic endings unique to each outcome, allowing players to uncover another layer of The Uprising’s story whether they emerge victorious as Rebels or successfully defend the kingdom as Kingsmen.”

Do you plan on playing The Uprising in Fortnite? Let us know in the comments.
